passage:
Thursday, late.
Forgot how to run the month-end reconciliation today. Sat at my desk with the spreadsheet open and my mind completely blank, even though I did it perfectly in March. Old me would have spiralled: "I'm losing it, I'm useless." Instead I opened my "How I did it" notes file, found the eight steps I'd written after last quarter, and was done in forty minutes. Alka from accounts peeked over and said, "You remember all that?" I laughed. "Nope. I remember where I wrote it." Brains aren't meant to hold every quarterly task; they drop what isn't used. I've set a reminder to skim the steps every six weeks so it's less of a shock. Honestly felt calm, which is new.
Dhruv

qa.q: How many steps were in Dhruv's notes?
qa.a: Eight steps.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel after finishing the reconciliation?
qa.a: Dhruv felt calm, which is new; instead of spiralling into "I'm useless", Dhruv treated the blank as normal and trusted the notes.

qa.q: What habit is Dhruv adding, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Skimming the steps every six weeks, so a rarely used task stays fresh and forgetting it is not a shock.

qa.q: How might Alka see Dhruv's approach?
qa.a: Alka seems impressed at first, assuming Dhruv remembered everything, and may learn that good notes matter more than a perfect memory.

grounding: An adult who forgets a rarely used task relies on notes and planned reviews, treating the forgetting as normal.

passage: The milk-collection centre in the village opened at six, and the fat-testing machine had been giving odd readings since the rains. Deepak knew it needed calibrating, but he had done that only once, last winter, and now his mind held nothing but a vague picture of a small screw. Farmers were already lining up with steel cans. His sister Arohi, who kept the register, saw him staring. "Forgot?" "Completely," he admitted, and for a second his ears burned. Then he pulled the tattered notebook from the drawer. Page three, in his own writing: "Calibration: warm the sample, test strip, turn the screw half a turn, test again." Ten minutes later the machine was right. "Write the date next to it," Arohi said. "And read it again before winter."

qa.q: What did page three of Deepak's notebook say?
qa.a: "Calibration: warm the sample, test strip, turn the screw half a turn, test again."

qa.q: What did Deepak feel when he couldn't remember the calibration?
qa.a: For a second he felt embarrassed, his ears burning, but he stayed calm because he trusted his notebook.

qa.q: What does Arohi suggest, and why?
qa.a: Write the date and read the notes again before winter, a review at intervals so the rarely used skill stays fresh.

qa.q: How might the farmers in line be affected by Deepak's notebook?
qa.a: They get accurate readings for their milk after only a short wait, instead of an operator guessing.

grounding: A working adult forgets a once-a-season task, uses his notes calmly, and plans a review, treating forgetting as normal.

passage: On the first Onam since the family moved to the kasba, Devika sat on the verandah making a small pookalam and sighing. "In my old school everyone was kind," she told her older brother Gautam. "We never fought. Not once." Gautam raised an eyebrow. "Remember when a girl in your row tore your notebook and you cried all the way home? And the boys who wouldn't let you play kho-kho?" Devika frowned at her petals. She did remember, a little, now that he said it. But in her mind the old classroom was sunny and full of laughter, and the new one was loud and strange. "Still," she said, "it was better." Gautam smiled and handed her a yellow flower.

qa.q: What was Devika making on the verandah?
qa.a: A small pookalam.

qa.q: Why does Devika insist the old school was better?
qa.a: She feels lonely and unsettled in the loud, strange new school, so distance makes the old class seem sunny and perfect and the quarrels fade.

qa.q: How could Gautam help Devika settle in?
qa.a: Gently remind her of both the good and hard parts of the old school, and help her notice small good things about the new one.

qa.q: How does Gautam see Devika's memory of her old school?
qa.a: He remembers the torn notebook and the kho-kho quarrel, so he sees her picture as rosier than it was, but he answers kindly.

grounding: A girl who has moved schools remembers her old class as perfect and forgets the quarrels.

passage: During Meskel week, Abebe's family lit a small bonfire in the yard of their new flat in Nairobi. Abebe watched the sparks and thought of his old school in Addis Ababa. "My old class was the best in the world," he told Fatima, the girl from next door who had come to watch. "Everyone shared their injera. Nobody ever got in trouble." Fatima tilted her head. "Nobody? Ever?" Abebe thought of the boy who used to hide his shoes, and the teacher who made him stand outside for talking. Those days felt far away and soft, like the fire's glow. "Almost nobody," he said. Fatima grinned. "My class hides shoes too. You could join our football game tomorrow."

qa.q: Where was Abebe's old school?
qa.a: In Addis Ababa.

qa.q: Why does Abebe say his old class was the best in the world?
qa.a: He misses home and feels a bit lonely in Nairobi, so distance makes the old class seem perfect; the shoe-hiding and being sent outside feel far away and soft.

qa.q: What small step from Fatima helps?
qa.a: Inviting him to tomorrow's football game gives him a way into the new place instead of only looking back.

qa.q: How might Fatima see Abebe's story about the best class?
qa.a: She finds it a bit too perfect but understands, and connects by saying her class hides shoes too.

grounding: A boy who moved away remembers his old class as perfect, forgetting the quarrels, during a festival in his new home.

passage: At the summer holiday camp in her new school, Gopika sat apart during craft hour. The camp counsellor knelt beside her. "Missing your old school?" "It was perfect there," Gopika said. "Everyone liked me. We never argued." A boy at the next table, Hrithik, looked up; he had moved from the same old school a year earlier. "Gopika, remember the class monitor fight? You didn't talk to anyone for a week." Gopika's cheeks went warm. She did remember, now. It seemed small and far away, like a faded picture. "That was only once," she muttered. The counsellor smiled. "Old places get prettier when we miss them. Want to make a card for someone new here?"

qa.q: What was Gopika doing during craft hour?
qa.a: Sitting apart.

qa.q: What did Gopika feel when Hrithik mentioned the monitor fight?
qa.a: Her cheeks went warm; she felt embarrassed and a bit defensive, because it didn't fit her perfect picture of the old school.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help, and what could come next?
qa.a: By saying old places get prettier when we miss them, and inviting her to make a card for someone new, a small step toward the present.

qa.q: What is it like for Hrithik to hear Gopika's version?
qa.a: He remembers the real quarrels, so he may feel he should be honest, and perhaps a bit amused.

grounding: A girl new to a school remembers her old class as perfect, forgetting the quarrels a former classmate recalls.

passage: Behind the family's kirana shop in Rajgarh, Anjali sat on a sack of rice with her physics book unopened. Between the shop counter, tuition and the entrance forms, every hour was spoken for. "Remember when we were small," she said to her cousin Disha, "and we spent whole days at Nani's farm, chasing goats? No worries at all." Disha, sorting coins, laughed softly. "You were terrified of the buffalo. And you cried whenever Nani made us come in before dark." Anjali paused. She had forgotten the buffalo. She had forgotten how small the world felt then, how she couldn't go anywhere without asking. Still, the ache stayed. "It feels lighter, in my head," she said. Disha nodded. "Maybe you need one light hour now, not the old days."

qa.q: Where did Anjali and Disha spend whole days as children?
qa.a: At Nani's farm.

qa.q: Why does Anjali still feel the ache after Disha reminds her?
qa.a: She feels overloaded and tired, so the farm days feel lighter in her head; comfort and loss colour the memory even when she recalls the buffalo.

qa.q: What could help Anjali now?
qa.a: As Disha suggests, carve out one light hour in the present rather than longing for the past, and perhaps talk to the family about the load.

qa.q: How does Disha see Anjali's longing?
qa.a: Disha remembers the fears and rules too, but responds with understanding rather than just correcting her.

grounding: A pressured teenager remembers childhood as carefree and forgets its fears and limits.

passage: Rania's alarm went off at five-thirty again, for the extra maths class before school in Amman. On the bus she scrolled through old family photos: herself as a little girl on the beach at Aqaba, sticky with ice cream, grinning. "Everything was so easy then," she said to her little brother Siddiq, who was half asleep against her shoulder. "Easy?" he mumbled. "Mama says you screamed every time a wave touched you. And you weren't allowed past the rocks." Rania looked closer at the photo. In the corner, barely visible, was her own hand gripping Baba's sleeve. She had forgotten the fear. But she still wanted, badly, to be back in that picture, where nobody asked about marks.

qa.q: Where was the beach photo taken?
qa.a: At Aqaba.

qa.q: Why does Rania long to be back in the photo?
qa.a: She is exhausted and pressured by early maths classes and marks, so childhood looks easy; comfort and loss colour the picture and hide her fear of the waves.

qa.q: What small step could help Rania with the present pressure?
qa.a: Talk with Mama or Baba about how heavy things feel, and find a small comfort now, rather than only escaping into old photos.

qa.q: How does Siddiq see Rania's easy childhood?
qa.a: Siddiq, repeating what Mama says, sees it more realistically: she was scared of the waves and not allowed past the rocks.

grounding: A pressured teenager longs for a carefree childhood, forgetting the fears and limits that were also there.

passage: Warden's note, week six. Vijay in Room 14 has gone home every weekend since term began, four hours by bus, and returns quieter each time. He talks about home and his school friends as if everything there was perfect. When I asked about the coding club he signed up for, he said, "I'll start once I'm settled." He has missed two lab sessions, both on Fridays before his bus. His love for home is real; I also wonder whether the trips help him avoid a hard new start here. I have asked Pooja, the student counsellor, to invite him for a chat, and I will pair him with a senior for Saturday lab practice.

qa.q: How long is Vijay's bus ride home?
qa.a: Four hours.

qa.q: What might Vijay be feeling when he talks about home?
qa.a: He is likely homesick and full of love for home, and also uneasy about the hard new start, which the weekend trips let him put off.

qa.q: What steps did the warden take, and why are they sensible?
qa.a: Asking Pooja, the counsellor, to invite him for a chat and pairing him with a senior for Saturday lab, which gently links him to the present without mocking his homesickness.

qa.q: What would change if Vijay joined the coding club this week?
qa.a: He would start to build friendships and routines at the hostel, which could make the new place feel less strange and home less of an escape.

grounding: A hostel student idealises home and goes back every weekend, with love mixed with avoiding the new challenges.

passage:
Sunday night, hostel.
Another group call with the old school gang. Everyone laughing about Class 12 like it was paradise: canteen samosas, cricket in the rain, no pressure. I miss it so much my chest hurts. Here the mess food is bland, the lectures are fast, and I still don't know anyone properly. Sahil from the next room asked if I wanted to join the quiz team. I said I was busy. I wasn't. I just stayed in bed and scrolled old photos. Writing it down, I can see it: Class 12 was also the year I barely slept and fought with Ammi about marks. Maybe I miss it because it's easier than being new. Tomorrow I'll tell Sahil yes. Maybe.
Farhan

qa.q: What did Sahil invite Farhan to join?
qa.a: The quiz team.

qa.q: What is Farhan feeling after the group call?
qa.a: Farhan feels homesick, with a chest-aching longing for school, and a little guilty about avoiding the new place by staying in bed.

qa.q: What is a small step Farhan could take?
qa.a: Tell Sahil yes tomorrow; one small connection here eases homesickness more than scrolling old photos.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel when Farhan says "busy"?
qa.a: Sahil might feel a bit rejected, or think Farhan isn't interested, without knowing about the homesickness.

grounding: A hostel student idealises school days and old friends, with homesick love mixed with avoiding new challenges.

passage: The power went off halfway through dinner at the family reunion in Nagpur, and in the candlelight Nitin mama started on his favourite theme. "In our time, everything was pure. Milk was real milk. Children respected elders. Nobody locked their doors." Anjali, who worked long days as a public health researcher, knew the harder story: more children fell ill then, and fewer girls went to school. She could feel the argument rising in her throat. Instead she watched his face, softened by the candle, and heard what was underneath: he missed his own mother's kitchen. "Tell me about Nani's milk," she said. Mama laughed and told a long story about a stubborn buffalo. When the lights came back, he was still talking, and so was everyone else.

qa.q: What did Nitin mama say about milk in his time?
qa.a: "Milk was real milk."

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling as the argument rose in her throat?
qa.a: She felt the urge to correct him, a flash of frustration, then tenderness as she saw that he missed his own mother's kitchen.

qa.q: Why did "Tell me about Nani's milk" work better than arguing?
qa.a: It honoured the warm memory without agreeing that the past was better, and kept the bond and the conversation going.

qa.q: What is it like for Nitin mama when Anjali asks about Nani's milk?
qa.a: He feels heard and happy, and tells a long story about a stubborn buffalo instead of defending his view.

grounding: A young professional hears an elder praise the old days, knows the past was harder, and listens kindly instead of arguing.

passage: At the office canteen in Pune, Sudha ma'am, three months from retirement, stirred her tea. "When I joined, we had real teamwork. No emails, no nonsense. We sorted everything over chai." Abhinav had heard from others that back then there was one phone for twenty people and reports were typed three times. He noticed she was smiling at something far away. "What was the best chai-time fix you remember?" he asked. Her eyes lit up. She described a night the whole team stayed late to retype a lost file, singing old songs. Abhinav listened, thinking it sounded exhausting and also lovely. He didn't correct her once. As they left, she patted his arm. "You're a good listener, beta."

qa.q: What did the team do on the night they stayed late?
qa.a: They retyped a lost file, singing old songs.

qa.q: What did Abhinav think while listening to Sudha ma'am's story?
qa.a: He thought it sounded exhausting and also lovely, and he felt warm toward her, so he chose not to correct her.

qa.q: What would you advise a young colleague in Abhinav's place?
qa.a: Ask about a favourite memory instead of disputing that things were better; you can know the past was harder and still enjoy the story.

qa.q: How does Sudha ma'am feel after the conversation?
qa.a: She feels appreciated and heard, patting his arm and calling him a good listener.

grounding: A young professional hears a senior praise the old days, knows they were harder, and listens kindly without arguing.

passage:
"Vishal, in my day a boy could buy a cinema ticket, a cold drink and a samosa for one rupee. Life was simple. People were honest."
"One rupee, Dadaji? That's amazing."
"And we walked everywhere. Nobody sat on phones all day."
"You walked to the mill every day, right? How far was it?"
"Eight kilometres each way. In the rain, in the heat."
"That sounds hard."
"Hard?" Dadaji paused. "Well... yes. My feet were always cracked. But we sang on the way, Ramesh and I."
"Ramesh dada, from the old photo?"
"Yes. My best friend. We sang the whole way."
"Will you sing me one of the songs?"
Dadaji cleared his throat and began, his eyes bright.

qa.q: How far did Dadaji walk to the mill each way?
qa.a: Eight kilometres.

qa.q: What might Vishal be feeling as Dadaji praises the old days?
qa.a: Vishal seems curious and affectionate, noticing the hardship behind the simple life but choosing warmth over correction.

qa.q: Which of Vishal's questions helped most, and why?
qa.a: "That sounds hard" and the request for a song: they let Dadaji admit the cracked feet himself and then share the warm part, with no argument.

qa.q: What is it like for Dadaji when Vishal asks for a song?
qa.a: He feels valued and happy, his eyes bright, remembering his friend Ramesh and the singing.

grounding: A young adult listens kindly to an elder's golden-age memories, noticing the hard parts without arguing.

passage:
Monday: After a draining first month at her new job, Sabina scrolls college photos on the metro home: the hostel terrace, midnight instant noodles, Baljeet's guitar. Her chest aches. "Those were the best years," she types to Baljeet, then deletes it.
Wednesday: Baljeet calls. They laugh about the terrace songs for an hour. Afterwards, Sabina writes two lists in her notebook: "What I loved then" and "What was also true then". The second list surprises her: the fees worry, the mess food, the exam-night panic, crying over her thesis.
Saturday: Sabina cooks the terrace-night noodles in her own small kitchen and invites two new colleagues. She tells them about the guitar songs, and also about thesis night. Her flat feels warmer than it did on Monday.

qa.q: What were the headings of Sabina's two lists?
qa.a: "What I loved then" and "What was also true then".

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling on the metro on Monday?
qa.a: Drained and a little lonely, with an ache for college that made her new life look poor by comparison.

qa.q: What did Sabina do that kept nostalgia healthy?
qa.a: She enjoyed the memories with Baljeet, listed the hard parts too, and then brought the good part, cooking and sharing stories, into her present.

qa.q: How might the new colleagues experience Saturday evening?
qa.a: They get a warm, honest invitation into Sabina's life, which may help them feel closer to her 😊

grounding: A wise adult enjoys nostalgia as comfort, reminds herself of what was hard, and brings the warmth into the present.

passage: Vijay, you keep saying school was better than your new job. Let me tell you about your Nandini nani at twenty-five. I had just moved to the city after my wedding, and I missed my village so much I made everyone around me miserable. "In the village the mangoes were sweeter, the people kinder," I'd say. One evening my mother-in-law asked, "Were they kinder when the well dried up and you walked two hours for water?" I was angry. But that night I wrote two lines in my diary: what I loved, and what was hard. Every year after, I read both. I still cook village food on Sundays, beta. But I stopped telling your nana the city was poor. It was only new.

qa.q: How long did Nandini walk for water when the well dried up?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: How did young Nandini feel when her mother-in-law asked about the well?
qa.a: She felt angry at first, then thoughtful enough to write down both what she loved and what was hard.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nandini's story?
qa.a: Writing the two lines in her diary that night and reading both every year, so she kept the comfort without calling the city poor.

qa.q: How might Nandini's mother-in-law have felt hearing the village praised?
qa.a: She may have felt tired of hearing the city run down, perhaps a little hurt, which is why she asked her sharp question.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to enjoy memories of her village while also remembering what was hard, so the present did not seem poor.

passage: Pallavi's train home for Diwali was cancelled at the last minute, and every other train was full. So she spent the evening alone in her rented room in Hyderabad, the neighbours' crackers booming. She let herself remember Diwali at home: rangoli with her mother, laddoos, cousins everywhere. Then, gently, she reminded herself of the rest: the cousins' fights, the aunties asking when she would marry, the year the power failed and nobody slept. The warmth was real, and so was the noise. She lit two diyas on her window ledge. When her friend Farida knocked with a box of kaju katli from her office, Pallavi laughed. "Now it's a festival," she said, making room on the floor.

qa.q: Why was Pallavi alone for Diwali?
qa.a: Her train home was cancelled at the last minute, and every other train was full.

qa.q: What might Pallavi have felt while the neighbours' crackers boomed?
qa.a: Lonely and homesick at first, then steadier as she enjoyed the memories and also remembered the hard parts.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do that stopped the past making the present feel poor?
qa.a: She enjoyed the warm memories, reminded herself of the fights and pressure, then made a small festival of her own with two diyas.

qa.q: What is it like for Farida when she knocks?
qa.a: Farida finds a welcoming friend who makes room on the floor, not someone sunk in regret, so the visit becomes a small celebration.

grounding: A wise adult enjoys festival nostalgia while remembering what was also hard, then makes the present warm.

passage: Last winter, on the day my best friend moved away, I sat on the step outside our flat and decided the whole week had been terrible. Maths test: bad. Lost my scarf: bad. Mummy was busy: bad. I told my sister Shalini that tomorrow would be terrible too. She sat next to me and asked, "Eshaan, what about the snowman cake on Tuesday?" I had forgotten it completely. And the kite on Wednesday. And winning at carrom. They were all there, but my sad feeling had hidden them. Now, when I'm sad, I try to remember one good thing from the week. It doesn't fix the sadness, but it makes tomorrow look less scary.

qa.q: What happened on Tuesday that Eshaan had forgotten?
qa.a: The snowman cake.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan decide the whole week had been terrible?
qa.a: Eshaan felt sad because the best friend moved away, and the sadness picked out only the bad memories and hid the good ones.

qa.q: What does Eshaan do now when feeling sad?
qa.a: Tries to remember one good thing from the week, which makes tomorrow look less scary.

qa.q: How does Shalini help, and what might she be feeling?
qa.a: She sits beside Eshaan and asks about the good moments, probably feeling caring and gentle rather than impatient.

grounding: A child who feels sad remembers only the bad parts of the week and expects tomorrow to be bad too.

passage: Teacher's note, monsoon term. Nilesh arrived soaked and silent today after his cycle chain broke on the way. At circle time he said, "This week was the worst. Everything went wrong." When I asked for examples, he listed only the broken chain, a low spelling score and losing at kabaddi. Rukmini reminded him that he had won the drawing prize on Monday. He shrugged: "That doesn't count." It seemed to me that his mood was choosing his memories. I sat with him and asked him to name one good thing from each day, and he found three. I will mention the tough week to his parents at pickup.

qa.q: What prize did Nilesh win on Monday?
qa.a: The drawing prize.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh say the drawing prize doesn't count?
qa.a: He was upset and gloomy after the broken chain, so his mood let only bad memories through and made the good one feel unimportant.

qa.q: How did the teacher help?
qa.a: By sitting with him and asking him to name one good thing from each day, so he found three, and by planning to tell his parents at pickup.

qa.q: What is it like for Rukmini when he shrugs off the prize?
qa.a: Rukmini tries to cheer him up and may feel confused or a little hurt that the reminder doesn't help.

grounding: A child in an upset mood recalls only the bad things from his week.

passage:

passage: Last term I went through weeks when everything looked grey. My friend Urmila would text "ok" and I'd read it as "I'm sick of you." A teacher said "see me after class" and I spent the whole period sure I was in trouble; she only wanted me for the quiz team. When I tried to think about the year, I remembered only failures: the maths paper, the missed goal, the day I cried on the bus. It all felt like plain fact, not a mood. My mother noticed I'd stopped eating breakfast and asked, "Swati, how long has it felt like this?" I said, "Weeks." That same evening she booked a time with the school counsellor. Talking helped me see the mood was painting everything. It still comes back sometimes, but now I tell someone.

qa.q: What did the teacher actually want after class?
qa.a: She wanted Swati for the quiz team.

qa.q: Why did Swati read Urmila's "ok" as "I'm sick of you"?
qa.a: Swati had been in a low, heavy mood for weeks, and that sadness turned neutral messages into rejection and made the judgment feel like plain fact.

qa.q: What made a difference, and what should someone in Swati's place do if the mood returns?
qa.a: Swati's mother noticed, asked, and booked the school counsellor that same evening; if it returns, telling a trusted adult or the counsellor early helps.

qa.q: How might Urmila have experienced those weeks?
qa.a: Urmila may have felt confused and hurt, sending ordinary "ok" texts without knowing they were being read as rejection.

grounding: A teenager in a low mood reads neutral messages as rejection and recalls only failures, and a parent arranges counselling support.

passage: Class teacher's note, Friday. For about three weeks Dilnaz has seemed low: head down, homework half done. Today Damini passed her a note about lunch, and Dilnaz read it and said, "She doesn't want me there." The note said, "Sitting by the tap today?" When I asked Dilnaz how the term had gone, she listed only mistakes and said it was "just a fact" that she was bad at everything. I told her I was glad she had talked to me, and that low moods can make things look darker than they are. With her agreement, I rang her father this afternoon, and I have booked her with the school counsellor for Monday morning. I will check in with her again before she leaves today.

qa.q: What did Damini's note actually say?
qa.a: "Sitting by the tap today?"

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz read the lunch note as rejection?
qa.a: She has felt low for about three weeks, and that heavy mood made a friendly note look like rejection and her mistakes look like fact.

qa.q: Which of the teacher's steps matter most?
qa.a: Listening without dismissing, explaining that low moods darken things, ringing her father that day, booking the counsellor, and checking in before she leaves.

qa.q: What is it like for Damini when her friendly note is taken badly?
qa.a: Damini may feel confused and hurt, since she meant to invite Dilnaz to lunch.

grounding: A teenager in a low mood reads a friendly note as rejection, and a teacher arranges caring adult and professional help.

passage:
Wednesday.
Nilesh didn't reply to my message about the project for five hours. Obviously he thinks I'm useless. Then Ma'am returned our essays and I only saw the red marks, not the "good ideas" at the top. At dinner I tried to list anything good from this month and couldn't. It's been like this for weeks, like grey glass over everything.
Later: Nilesh finally replied: "sorry, phone died, your part's great." So I was wrong about him. That scared me more, honestly: how sure I felt. I showed this page to Mumma. She held my hand and said we'll see the school counsellor together, and she'll ring the doctor tomorrow too. I feel a bit lighter just telling her.
Shreya

qa.q: What was Nilesh's reply?
qa.a: "Sorry, phone died, your part's great."

qa.q: Why did Shreya feel so sure that Nilesh thought Shreya was useless?
qa.a: A low mood lasting weeks, like grey glass over everything, made the silence feel like rejection; how certain it felt scared Shreya once the real reply came.

qa.q: What did Shreya do that was wise?
qa.a: Showed the diary page to Mumma, who planned to see the school counsellor together and ring the doctor; a low mood that lasts needs caring adults and professional help.

qa.q: How might Mumma feel reading the page?
qa.a: She is likely worried and tender, holding Shreya's hand, and glad to have been told.

grounding: A teenager in a long low mood misreads a delayed reply as rejection and turns to a parent for support.

passage: Karthik, you asked how I ended up with four commitments in one week? Okay. It was the day I got the internship offer. I was flying. Wasim the unstoppable, right? So when the fest team asked me to run the stall, I said yes. When my cousin asked for help shifting his flat on Saturday, yes. When our professor needed a volunteer for the conference, yes, obviously. And that bike trip to the hills with you lot on Sunday? Yes, even though my bike needs new brakes. In that mood nothing looked hard or risky. It all looked fun! Then Thursday came. I was exhausted, and I realised I'd forgotten my own assignment. So I've cancelled the bike trip, sorry, and I'm getting the brakes fixed first.

qa.q: What was wrong with Wasim's bike?
qa.a: It needed new brakes.

qa.q: Why did Wasim say yes to everything that day?
qa.a: Wasim felt elated and unstoppable after the internship offer, so every task looked fun and nothing looked risky.

qa.q: What could Wasim try the next time good news arrives?
qa.a: Wait a day before saying yes to new commitments, and weigh each one, especially risks like the brakes, when calmer.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel about the cancelled bike trip?
qa.a: Karthik may be disappointed but relieved too, since riding with bad brakes was a real danger that Wasim's mood had hidden.

grounding: A young adult in a great mood says yes to too much and overlooks a real risk.

passage:
Friday: Arnab's short film wins the college prize. He is buzzing. At the party, his friend Noor asks if he'll co-host the fest, edit her documentary and join a road trip to the beach, driving there and back the same night. "Yes, yes, yes!" he laughs. Everything feels easy.
Tuesday: The co-hosting rehearsal clashes with the documentary edit. He hasn't slept properly in three days. The road trip is Thursday, and he realises he would be driving eight hours overnight, exhausted.
Thursday: Arnab texts Noor: "Sorry, I said yes while I was floating. I can do the edit, not the co-hosting, and not the night drive. Driving that tired isn't safe." Noor replies with a thumbs-up. He sleeps for ten hours.

qa.q: How long would the overnight drive have been?
qa.a: Eight hours.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when he said yes three times at the party?
qa.a: He felt buzzing and elated after the prize, so everything felt easy and risks like a tired night drive did not register.

qa.q: What did Arnab do right on Thursday?
qa.a: He reassessed calmly, kept one commitment, and cancelled the co-hosting and the unsafe night drive, explaining honestly.

qa.q: How might Noor see Arnab's change of plan?
qa.a: She accepts it easily with a thumbs-up, probably glad he was honest rather than letting her down at the last minute.

grounding: A young adult in a great mood underestimates a risk and overcommits, then reconsiders when calmer.

passage: Pradeep, you have the face of someone who got good news and said yes to everything. I know that face. At twenty-one, your Sonali bua got her first job letter, and the same evening my college friends asked me to lead a trek up the ghats in the middle of the monsoon. I said yes before they finished the sentence. I also said yes to organising my cousin's engagement and to teaching a weekend class. In that happy haze, rain looked romantic, not dangerous. It was my father who asked quietly, "Have you heard the landslide warning on the radio?" I hadn't. We moved the trek to October. That very week, a road on that route was closed by a landslide. Joy is a lovely feeling, beta, but a poor judge of risk.

qa.q: When did they move the trek to?
qa.a: October.

qa.q: Why did young Sonali say yes before her friends finished the sentence?
qa.a: She was joyful after her first job letter, and in that happy haze the monsoon rain looked romantic rather than dangerous.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Her father's quiet question about the landslide warning, which made her check the risk and move the trek.

qa.q: How might Sonali's father have felt watching her say yes to everything?
qa.a: He was probably happy for her but quietly worried, which is why he asked about the warning instead of scolding.

grounding: An elder recalls how a great mood made her underestimate the risk of a monsoon trek and say yes to too much.

passage: In the staff room after the meeting, Leela's hands were shaking. The principal had moved her Class 10 section to a new teacher without a word to her. She opened her laptop and typed fast: a resignation letter, sharp and complete. Charu, marking papers across the table, looked up. "You okay?" "No," Leela said. "I'm furious. Which is exactly why I'm not sending this tonight." She saved it as a draft and wrote on a sticky note: "Reread Thursday." On Thursday morning, calmer after two nights' sleep, she read it again. Parts were true; parts were just heat. She deleted the letter and asked the principal for a half-hour meeting about the change instead.

qa.q: What did Leela write on the sticky note?
qa.a: "Reread Thursday."

qa.q: How was Leela feeling when she typed the resignation letter?
qa.a: She was furious and shaken, her hands trembling, after her section was moved without a word.

qa.q: Which of Leela's choices was wisest, and why?
qa.a: Saving the letter as a draft and rereading it after two nights, so she could separate the true points from the heat and ask for a meeting instead.

qa.q: How might Charu see Leela's decision not to send it?
qa.a: Charu probably feels relieved and a bit impressed, having seen how upset Leela was.

grounding: An adult notices her anger, postpones a major decision, and returns when calm to see if her view has changed.

passage:
Dear Kamal bhai,
Last week I almost did something I'd have regretted. After the job rejection on Monday, I felt hopeless, and at midnight I drafted a message to the Pune firm turning down their offer too, saying I wasn't good enough for anything. It felt like a clear decision. It wasn't; it was despair wearing a suit. I remembered what Ammi always says: sleep on the big ones. So I closed the laptop. On Wednesday I reread the draft and barely recognised the voice. I've accepted the Pune offer. I'm writing this so you'll remind me next time: when I'm that low, I don't decide, I wait. Thank you for listening on the phone that night.
Your sister,
Nazia

qa.q: When did Nazia reread the draft?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling at midnight after the rejection?
qa.a: She felt hopeless and not good enough, and in that despair a big decision looked clear.

qa.q: What rule is Nazia asking Kamal to remind her of?
qa.a: When she is that low, she doesn't decide, she waits, and comes back to big choices when calmer.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel reading the email?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and trusted, glad his phone call helped and that she asked him to be her reminder.

grounding: An adult notices despair shaping a major decision, waits, and returns calm enough to choose differently.

passage: You want to know my rule, Anirban? Ganga's forty-eight-hour rule. It came from the worst night of my life. My sister and I fought about who would look after Amma after her operation, and I was so angry I wrote her a message that would have ended us. Every word felt true. I had my thumb over send. Then I noticed my jaw aching, my heart hammering, and I thought: this isn't me deciding, this is the anger deciding. So I put the phone in the cupboard. Two days later I read it again. Half of it was cruel and not even accurate. I deleted it, called her instead, and we worked out a rota. So now, when I'm furious or hopeless, I don't send, I don't sign, I don't quit. I wait, then look again.

qa.q: Where did Ganga put the phone?
qa.a: In the cupboard.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling with a thumb over send?
qa.a: Ganga was furious, jaw aching and heart hammering, and every angry word felt true in that moment.

qa.q: What is Ganga's rule, and why does it work?
qa.a: The forty-eight-hour rule: no sending, signing or quitting while furious or hopeless, then looking again once calm, when the view is often different.

qa.q: What would have changed for Ganga's sister if the message had been sent?
qa.a: She would have received cruel, inaccurate words that could have ended the relationship, instead of a call and a shared rota.

grounding: An adult notices anger shaping a message, postpones it, and returns calm to find the view has changed.
